This document covers the skills of the `core-tools` module: what each one is for and when to recommend it.

## How the core tools fit

The core tools belong to no phase and no path. Each stands alone and works with or without any other module. Suggest one whenever it would help: before, during, after, or entirely outside another module's flow. Never present one as a required step. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed.

## Initiatives

An initiative is one body of work of any kind: a product, a feature, a book, a set of art assets. Its folder under `output_folder` holds what every module's skills write for that work. `active_initiative` under `[core]` in `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` names the folder in use; the file is personal, so each person can work on a different one. With none active, work is written loose to `{output_folder}/`, and some skills first ask whether it belongs to an initiative. The `bmad` skill shows, switches, creates, or clears the active initiative. What goes inside the folder is up to each module: its help says.

## Start here

- No idea yet, or wants more and better ideas on a topic → `bmad-brainstorming`.
- Has an idea and is not sure it holds up → `bmad-forge-idea`.
- Needs facts from outside before deciding (a market, a technology, competitors, what users say), has a research report to make usable, or wants their own code researched (how something works, why it is built that way, the code a ticket depends on) → `bmad-deep-recon`.
- Needs to write a document: a decision record or ADR, a postmortem, a proposal or grant application, a security review or threat model, a pitch deck or talk, or any document from the team's own template → `bmad-facilitate`. A PRD goes to John (`bmad-agent-pm`); a product brief, PRFAQ or BRD to Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`).
- Has a piece of work and wants it better:
  - They have a draft in front of them (theirs or the model's) and want it pushed further, or want a critique method run on it → `bmad-advanced-elicitation`. It starts only by name: tell them to say "advanced elicitation", with the method if they have one in mind.
  - They ask for a review of a diff, a file, or a document → `bmad-review`.
  - They want several points of view arguing it out, a roundtable, or a focus group of their customers → `bmad-party-mode`.
- Has large or raw input:
  - A transcript, a chat or email thread, a voice memo, or a long document they want what matters from (decisions, action items, key points) → `bmad-ingest`.
  - A document past about 50 KB that agents work from (an old spec, a vendor manual, a large PRD), or one already sharded that they want to change → `bmad-shard-pro`. A long document that is kept and edited is split; one that has to stay one file, or a fixed reference, gets a contents list (`help/shard-pro.md`). A document under about 50 KB needs nothing, including one a planning skill just wrote.
  - About to start a PRD, brief, architecture or tickets with large inputs: suggest preparing them first, raw inputs through `bmad-ingest` and documents past about 50 KB through `bmad-shard-pro`, so the planning skill reads short notes and only the parts it needs.
  - A sharded document is the input to another skill: give that skill the folder's main file, named after the folder, which links to every shard.
- BMad itself needs attention:
  - Something was installed or updated, or a skill reports that BMad is not set up or a BMad script was not found → `bmad setup`.
  - "What do I have, and is it current?" → `bmad status`.
  - Which initiative is active, or they want to switch, create, or clear one → `bmad`.
  - They want a skill, an agent or a document it writes to behave differently, such as a section the PRD must have, HTML by default, or the team's own template → `bmad-customize`. They need not know which skill writes the document.
  - They ask what a BMad module is or how to make one → `help/modules.md`.

The method turns an intent of any size into working software. Recommend the smallest path that safely fits the work; never march the user through every skill. **The ticket is the spec.** The initiative, epic or story file is the spec at its level. Every skill that works on a ticket reads it first and in full and trusts it; its `sources:` are re-read only by Sofia when she updates it, and a `companions:` file only where the ticket points. ===== core-tools -- module core-tools -- path help/help.md -- reported_from bmod-core-tools -- content # BMad Core Tools knowledge This document covers the skills of the `core-tools` module: what each one is for and when to recommend it. ## How the core tools fit The core tools belong to no phase and no path. Each stands alone and works with or without any other module. Suggest one whenever it would help: before, during, after, or entirely outside another module's flow. Never present one as a required step. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed. ## Initiatives An initiative is one body of work of any kind: a product, a feature, a book, a set of art assets. Its folder under `output_folder` holds what every module's skills write for that work. `active_initiative` under `[core]` in `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` names the folder in use; the file is personal, so each person can work on a different one. With none active, work is written loose to `{output_folder}/`, and some skills first ask whether it belongs to an initiative. The `bmad` skill shows, switches, creates, or clears the active initiative. What goes inside the folder is up to each module: its help says. ## Start here - No idea yet, or wants more and better ideas on a topic → `bmad-brainstorming`. - Has an idea and is not sure it holds up → `bmad-forge-idea`. - Needs facts from outside before deciding (a market, a technology, competitors, what users say), has a research report to make usable, or wants their own code researched (how something works, why it is built that way, the code a ticket depends on) → `bmad-deep-recon`. - Needs to write a document: a decision record or ADR, a postmortem, a proposal or grant application, a security review or threat model, a pitch deck or talk, or any document from the team's own template → `bmad-facilitate`. A PRD goes to John (`bmad-agent-pm`); a product brief, PRFAQ or BRD to Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`). - Has a piece of work and wants it better: - They have a draft in front of them (theirs or the model's) and want it pushed further, or want a critique method run on it → `bmad-advanced-elicitation`. It starts only by name: tell them to say "advanced elicitation", with the method if they have one in mind. - They ask for a review of a diff, a file, or a document → `bmad-review`. - They want several points of view arguing it out, a roundtable, or a focus group of their customers → `bmad-party-mode`. - Has large or raw input: - A transcript, a chat or email thread, a voice memo, or a long document they want what matters from (decisions, action items, key points) → `bmad-ingest`. - A document past about 50 KB that agents work from (an old spec, a vendor manual, a large PRD), or one already sharded that they want to change → `bmad-shard-pro`. A long document that is kept and edited is split; one that has to stay one file, or a fixed reference, gets a contents list (`help/shard-pro.md`). A document under about 50 KB needs nothing, including one a planning skill just wrote. - About to start a PRD, brief, architecture or tickets with large inputs: suggest preparing them first, raw inputs through `bmad-ingest` and documents past about 50 KB through `bmad-shard-pro`, so the planning skill reads short notes and only the parts it needs. - A sharded document is the input to another skill: give that skill the folder's main file, named after the folder, which links to every shard. - BMad itself needs attention: - Something was installed or updated, or a skill reports that BMad is not set up or a BMad script was not found → `bmad setup`. - "What do I have, and is it current?" → `bmad status`. - Which initiative is active, or they want to switch, create, or clear one → `bmad`. - They want a skill, an agent or a document it writes to behave differently, such as a section the PRD must have, HTML by default, or the team's own template → `bmad-customize`. It does not judge ideas until asked to converge. Sessions resume. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/brainstorm-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `brainstorm.html` and, on request, `brainstorm-.md`: the chosen ideas, ready as input to any installed planning skill. | | `bmad-forge-idea` | Questions one half-formed idea hard until the user can act on it or drop it. | Any idea, not only products, including a change to an existing project. It ends hardened, killed, or clearer, and all three are good outcomes. Not for generating ideas or for outside facts. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/forge-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `forge-report.html` and, when the idea hardens, `forge-.md`: the surviving decisions, ready as input to any installed planning or build skill. | | `bmad-deep-recon` | Research that serves a decision, with cited sources found now, never from memory. | It can draft a prompt for the user's own research tool, process a finished report, or run the research here. It can also choose between candidates, or answer questions about this repository from its code and git history. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/research-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `brief.md` and `research-.md`, which is input for whatever skill acts on the decision. Codebase research also writes each ADR the user approves, beside the code it governs. | | `bmad-facilitate` | Coaches the user through one document from a template library, then updates or validates it later. | Its templates come from installed modules: Method's `decision-record`, `postmortem` and `security-review`, Founder's `proposal` and `pitch-deck`, and the Creative Intelligence Suite's `character`, from CIS 0.4.0. A team adds or replaces templates and adds rules to shipped ones. Rigor follows the stakes the user states. Unfinished runs resume. Other skills can call it on their inputs. | The original, unchanged, in `{output_folder}/raw/`; the note in the calling skill's folder, such as a PRD's `sources/`, else `{output_folder}/notes/`. | | `bmad-customize` | Changes how an installed skill or agent behaves without editing it: persona, standing facts, templates, output paths, steps on completion, and what a document such as the PRD asks for, contains or renders. | Team overrides are committed and shared; personal ones are not. Central config is edited by hand. | `{project-root}/_bmad/custom/{skill-name}.toml` for the team, `{skill-name}.user.toml` for one person; a document change in `{project-root}/_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`. | ## `bmad`: setup, status, and help - `bmad setup` creates and repairs `{project-root}/_bmad`, including the shared scripts other skills call, and asks each installed module's new configuration questions. Recommend it after anything is installed or updated. - `bmad status` changes nothing. To use it in another repository, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD` there, then `bmad setup`. ## More detail This document should be enough to route the user and say what to do next. The source repository it links to is the final authority on how anything actually behaves. ===== method -- module method -- path help/help.md -- reported_from bmod-method -- content # BMad Method knowledge This document covers the skills of the `method` module: what each one gives the user, when to recommend it, and what to offer next. ## How the method works The method turns an intent of any size into working software. Recommend the smallest path that safely fits the work; never march the user through every skill. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed, and say plainly when a step has no installed skill rather than inventing a substitute. **The ticket is the spec.** The initiative, epic or story file is the spec at its level. Every skill that works on a ticket reads it first and in full and trusts it; its `sources:` are re-read only by Sofia when she updates it, and a `companions:` file only where the ticket points. Talk to Sofia the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`) to fill its Requirements from whatever the user has (a PRD, a brief, notes, a transcript), keep it in step with its sources, and slice from it. A transcript, a chat or email thread, or a voice memo goes through `bmad-ingest` first when it is installed, and the note it returns is the input. A sharded document is given to any skill as its main file, named after its folder, which links to every shard. The method adds note templates for `standup`, `retrospective` (the meeting, not `bmad-retrospective`'s epic review), `sprint-review`, `discovery-workshop` and `user-interview`. The four phases are analysis (ideation, research, is it worth building), planning (what exactly, and in what slices), implementation (build it), and validation (is it right). They describe what kind of help a skill gives. They are not a mandatory sequence to complete. Project size decides how many build sessions the work needs. Stakes decide how heavy the planning gets. A large hobby project keeps planning light; a small change to a regulated system may not. ## More detail This document should be enough to route the user and say what to do next. **No input.** Ask for a file path, pasted content, an explanation, or a source.

## Memory and derivation

`.memlog.md` is append-only, one line per entry; requirements carry their stable `R<n>`. Each run derives the derived lines and every spec-authored companion from the memlog plus the sources it cites.

On a container, SPEC is the only writer of the derived lines; a change goes to the memlog, never into them by hand. A derive replaces exactly those lines, sets `sources:` and `companions:` in the frontmatter, adds a References line per companion, and touches nothing else. A source id on a line must exist in a `sources:` file; neither list names the memlog, README files or process records.

Writes go through `{project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py`:

- `uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py init --workspace <ticket folder> --field topic="<the ticket's title>"` — once, at create.
- `uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py append --workspace <ticket folder> --type <decision|constraint|requirement|assumption|question|direction|note|event> --text "<one-line gist, reason included>"` — one per line; batch them in one shell call per section.
- Terminal moments (a validation verdict, "spec finalized") are `--type event` entries; the memlog has no status field.

## The Operation

Read the input and what it links. With a `.memlog.md`, this is an update: read the memlog, the authority on decisions and requirement ids, and re-read every file in `sources:`; preserve the ids and give new requirements the next unused `R<n>`. A ticket with Requirements lines and no memlog is also an update: `memlog.py init`, then append each existing derived line as its own entry, ids kept. Otherwise this is a create. An epic whose refinement settled that its parent's lines are its only input (the ids its `covers` names) gets one line per parent id, `R<n> (parent R<m>)`, in the parent's words, with no elicitation, self-validate or memlog; when the parent changes, its lines are re-rendered from the parent, ids kept.

A claim is **load-bearing** if any consumer (downstream skill, implementing agent, verification pass) would change a decision without it.

When the ticket is a container, offer to slice per `slice.md`, or to re-slice what went stale. On the repo store, save it through `write` per `board.md`; on a tracker it stays in the tree until published.

5. **Seeing availability:** *My pick: a day view showing each room's booked and free slots.*
6. **What's out for the first version?** *My pick: recurring meetings, calendar sync (Google or Outlook), email notifications and a mobile app are all out.*

It's a hobby project.

# Board

Read a ticket, and its remote state if published, before changing it. Commit changed files on the current branch when `output_folder` is in a git repo; never push.

## Reading the tree

- `find`'s `<ref>` is `<epic id>.<entry id>`, an entry id with its epic folder, a tracker id, a file name, or an unbroken title phrase; for looser words, pick from `status`, asking when several fit. Its `story_file` is null until pulled; `plan` is the plan's path, existing or not.
- `tickets.py next [<folder>]` groups open tickets by next step; `tickets.py status [<folder>]` lists every ticket.
- `<folder>` is an epic folder name, `backlog`, or the initiative, by default the active one, where `next` and `status` add a `backlog` key to show. On a parent initiative they list its child initiatives under `initiatives`.
- With a tracker, sync first (Tracker sync) and pass `--synced` to `next`.

Act with the user on any non-empty key:

- `unpinned_after`: add the epic's `after` prerequisite to the entry that needs it.
- `undeclared_after`: add the awaited epic, with its `needs`, to its epic's `after` in the breakdown, or drop the prerequisite.
- `order_conflict`: reorder or merge the epics, or record why in a `Decision:` line.
- `drift`: make the leaf file's and the entry's `after` or `hitl` equal.
- `problems`: an orphan plan gets its `ticket` set to the entry id or file stem; an unknown status is fixed with `mark`.
- `waiting_on` on a `blocked` row: say what the ticket waits on.
- `unknown` on a `blocked` row: settle it, remove it, and add a dated `Decision:` line to the file's Notes, or its epic's when it has no file.

## Publish

On the repo store, approval commits (Conventions in `workflow.md`) and `publication` does not apply. On a tracker, publication is `at_inception`: `at_inception` offers to publish the agreed set after validation; `on_start` publishes each ticket when it starts. An explicit user request overrides it.

Publish to a tracker through `write`:

- Write the leaf's file first (`tickets.py pull` if none); send it minus the frontmatter lines `tracker_id`, `remote`, `tracker_status`, `status`, and `assignee`.
- Create parents and prerequisites first, adding local prerequisites to the scope. An `after` naming a sibling's id or `<epic id>.<entry id>` is that entry's remote item; `epic-<slug>` is the epic's.
- A type mapped to `""` is never sent; its children attach to the nearest published ancestor. Say so once.
- Offer `setup` at first publish, or when the tracker lacks something the maps or `fields` name.
- Then mirror, and edit a published container's `tracker_id` and `remote` into its file.

An unrefined ticket may be published with `refined: false`; refinement updates the same file and remote item.

## Start

Offer the first `ready_to_start` row of `next` in build order, or every unassigned one when work can run in parallel. `find` it with the row's `ref`, refine a `ready_to_refine` one first per `ticket.md`, and confirm it is unassigned; the builder reads the ticket. With the user's approval, start it: on a tracker, publish it if needed, `write` it to `[tickets.status].in-progress` and mirror; on the repo store, write nothing. Then hand it to `bmad-build` or `bmad-build-auto`.

Only an unattended run's orchestrator honors the row's `plan_checkpoint` and `done_checkpoint`.

## Status

The plan is `<type>-<slug>-plan.md` beside where the leaf's file is or would be, linked by its `ticket`; the leaf file's `status` counts only without a plan.

The builds write `draft` through `built`, and `bmad-build-auto` writes `blocked` when it halts; an orchestrator may set `done` through `mark`. Sofia sets `done`, `dropped`, or an assignee only when the user says so (a ticket done or dropped, or a person working it by hand).

- **Tracker.** `write` transitions the item to `[tickets.status].<state>`, with `<state>` as `tickets.py status` reports it, never a `status` word, and sets its assignee; then mirror. `mark` refuses a tracker store.
- **Waiting on a person or an answer** on the repo store: `mark` with the current status (`draft` when none) and `--blocked <reason>`; a `mark` without it clears the block.
- **A container's** `status` is Sofia's to edit in its file: absent until its first ticket starts, then `in-progress`, then `done` or `dropped` on the user's confirmation; a published one transitions through `write`.

## Close, drop, move

- Closing every child does not close the parent. Run the closure check in `validate.md` against its requirements and Done when; the user confirms completion.
- Drop only after a `Dropped:` line in the ticket's Notes, or its epic's when it has no file, says why; then set `dropped` per Status, or on a tracker an unpublished entry takes `tracker_status: dropped` through `mirror`. Never delete an entry from an approved `tickets.toml`. With the user, remove or repoint the dropped ticket in each dependent's `after` (`status` lists them under `blocks`). Cancelling a container cancels its descendants once the user confirms.
- Move an entry with `tickets.py move`; it renumbers the entry, moves its file and plan, rewrites every `after` naming it, and reports what it rewrote. It lands last in the destination's `tickets.toml`; put it in build order by hand. Move its `covers` ids between the two epics with the user if the requirement moves. An epic moves as its whole folder with its `[[epic]]` table. Then run `tickets.py status` on the initiative and clear what it reports.
- A done standalone ticket stays in `backlog/` beside its plan.

## Tracker sync

After every `write`, and after the `query` before a board view, run `tickets.py mirror [<folder>]` with a JSON array on stdin, one object per ticket: `ref` (or its `tracker_id`) plus any of `tracker_id`, `remote`, `tracker_status`, `assignee`, `after`.

- `tracker_status` is the state mapped back through `[tickets.status]`: after `write`, the state sent; when two states share a tracker status the query cannot tell apart, the current one if it matches, else the earlier.
- `after` holds tracker ids as strings; an empty string removes a key's line.
- A tracker leaf missing from the tree, even one a known ticket's `after` names, comes back under `unmatched`: add an `[[entry]]` to the parent's `tickets.toml` (the folder's `next_id`, the item's type and title, a one-sentence description), mirror again with that `ref`, and put the item's body in the pulled file.
- Query published containers with their leaves; `mirror` reports them under `containers`, never `unmatched`; tell the user when one's tracker status differs from its file's, and close one only through the closure check.
- A body that differs from the file: show both and ask.
- Move a ticket the tracker shows under another parent per Close, drop, move, then mirror again.
- A failed store call: tell the user what blocks it, confirm the setup, and ask them to authenticate if that is the cause. An empty verb field you cannot infer: ask, and offer to record it per `store-setup.md`.

# Meeting room booker — the idea, as the owner stated it (2026-11-12)

## ¶1
A simple web page where office staff can see which meeting rooms are free today, and book one.

## ¶2
Five rooms: Room 1-5, seating 4, 4, 6, 8 and 12.

## ¶3
To book, you click a free slot and give your name, a meeting title and a length from 30 minutes to 2 hours.

## ¶4
Two bookings in the same room must never overlap. A meeting ending at 11:00 and one starting at 11:00 is fine.

## ¶5
If two people book the same slot at the same moment, one wins and the other sees "This slot has just been booked."

## ¶6
Tech: Python with FastAPI, a SQLite database, running on my own computer.

## ¶7
Not included: login, repeat bookings, editing, cancelling, time zones, mobile.

## ¶8
It's a hobby project.
EOF
W=_bmad-output/initiative-meeting-room-booker
M="uv run _bmad/scripts/memlog.py"
$M init --workspace $W --field topic="Meeting Room Booker" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE
$M append --workspace $W --type direction --text "Source: owner's stated idea, saved verbatim to _bmad-output/raw/idea-meeting-room-booker.md (paragraphs ¶1-¶8)" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE
$M append --workspace $W --type requirement --text "R1 (idea ¶1): one web page shows, for today, which of the rooms are free and which are booked, slot by slot" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE
$M append --workspace $W --type requirement --text "R2 (idea ¶2): the page lists exactly five rooms, Room 1-5, with seats 4, 4, 6, 8 and 12" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE
$M append --workspace $W --type requirement --text "R3 (idea ¶3): clicking a free slot lets a person book it with their name, a meeting title and a length from 30 minutes to 2 hours; the booking then shows as booked" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE
$M append --workspace $W --type requirement --text "R4 (idea ¶4): two bookings in the same room never overlap; one ending at 11:00 and one starting at 11:00 is allowed" 2>&1 | grep -v UV_NATIVE

# Meeting Room Booker

## Description

A single web page, run on the owner's computer, where office staff see which of the five meeting rooms are free today and book a free slot by giving their name, a meeting title and a length. The one rule that must never break is that bookings in a room do not overlap, even when two people book the same slot at once. It is a hobby project: the scope is the owner's stated idea (`_bmad-output/raw/idea-meeting-room-booker.md`) and nothing more.

## Outcome

For office staff, finding and booking a free room for today takes one page and a few clicks, and no room is ever double-booked: shown by the Done when checks passing on the owner's computer.

## Requirements

- R1 (idea ¶1): One web page shows, for today, which rooms are free and which are booked, slot by slot.
- R2 (idea ¶2): The page lists exactly five rooms, Room 1–5, seating 4, 4, 6, 8 and 12.
- R3 (idea ¶3): Clicking a free slot lets a person book it with their name, a meeting title and a length from 30 minutes to 2 hours; the booking then shows as booked.
- R4 (idea ¶4): Two bookings in the same room never overlap; one ending at 11:00 and one starting at 11:00 is allowed.
- R5 (idea ¶5): When two people book the same slot at the same moment, exactly one booking is stored and the other sees "This slot has just been booked."

## Constraints

- C1 (idea ¶6): Python with FastAPI and a SQLite database, running on the owner's own computer.
- C2 (idea ¶7, ¶8): Hobby scale; nothing is built for login, repeat bookings, editing, cancelling, time zones or mobile.

## Done when

- Started on the owner's computer, the page shows Room 1–5 with their seat counts and today's free and booked slots.
- A booking made by clicking a free slot and filling in name, title and length shows as booked after a page reload.
- An automated test shows an overlapping booking in the same room is refused and a back-to-back one (ends 11:00, starts 11:00) is accepted.
- An automated test fires two simultaneous bookings for the same slot: exactly one is stored and the other gets "This slot has just been booked."

## Boundaries

- Out: login or accounts, repeat bookings, editing or cancelling a booking, time zones (all times are the computer's local time), mobile layout, hosting anywhere but the owner's computer.
- Tracer path: open the page → see today's grid of five rooms → click a free slot → submit name, title and length → booking stored in SQLite → grid shows the slot booked.

- source — _bmad-output/raw/idea-meeting-room-booker.md, ¶1–¶8

- Assumption: The bookable day is 08:00–18:00 in the computer's local time, and a booking must end by 18:00.
- Assumption: Slots start on the half hour, and lengths go in 30-minute steps (30, 60, 90, 120 minutes).

- Assumption: The five rooms are fixed seed data, with no screen to add or edit them.
- Open question: Does a booked slot show the booker's name and title to everyone, or only that it is taken? Waits: the page design.

# Meeting Room Booker

## Description

A single web page, run on the owner's computer, where office staff see which of the five meeting rooms are free today and book a free slot by giving their name, a meeting title and a length. The one rule that must never break is that bookings in a room do not overlap, even when two people book the same slot at once. It is a hobby project: the scope is the owner's stated idea (`_bmad-output/raw/idea-meeting-room-booker.md`) and nothing more.

## Outcome

For office staff, finding and booking a free room for today takes one page and a few clicks, and no room is ever double-booked: shown by the Done when checks passing on the owner's computer.

## Requirements

- R1 (idea ¶1): One web page shows, for today, which rooms are free and which are booked, slot by slot.
- R2 (idea ¶2): The page lists exactly five rooms, Room 1–5, seating 4, 4, 6, 8 and 12.
- R3 (idea ¶3): Clicking a free slot lets a person book it with their name, a meeting title and a length from 30 minutes to 2 hours; the booking then shows as booked.
- R4 (idea ¶4): Two bookings in the same room never overlap; one ending at 11:00 and one starting at 11:00 is allowed.
- R5 (idea ¶5): When two people book the same slot at the same moment, exactly one booking is stored and the other sees "This slot has just been booked."

## Constraints

- C1 (idea ¶6): Python with FastAPI and a SQLite database, running on the owner's own computer.
- C2 (idea ¶7, ¶8): Hobby scale; nothing is built for login, repeat bookings, editing, cancelling, time zones or mobile.

## Done when

- Started on the owner's computer, the page shows Room 1–5 with their seat counts and today's free and booked slots.
- A booking made by clicking a free slot and filling in name, title and length shows as booked after a page reload.
- An automated test shows an overlapping booking in the same room is refused and a back-to-back one (ends 11:00, starts 11:00) is accepted.
- An automated test fires two simultaneous bookings for the same slot: exactly one is stored and the other gets "This slot has just been booked."

## Boundaries

- Out: login or accounts, repeat bookings, editing or cancelling a booking, time zones (all times are the computer's local time), mobile layout, hosting anywhere but the owner's computer.
- Tracer path: open the page → see today's grid of five rooms → click a free slot → submit name, title and length → booking stored in SQLite → grid shows the slot booked.

## References

- source — _bmad-output/raw/idea-meeting-room-booker.md, ¶1–¶8

## Notes

- Decision (2026-11-12): The bookable day is 08:00–18:00 in the computer's local time, and a booking must end by 18:00.
- Decision (2026-11-12): Slots start on the half hour, and lengths are 30, 60, 90 or 120 minutes.
- Decision (2026-11-12): Only today can be viewed and booked, and slots already past cannot be booked.
- Decision (2026-11-12): The five rooms are fixed seed data, with no screen to add or edit them.
- Decision (2026-11-12): A booked slot shows the booker's name and meeting title to everyone; with no login it is the only way to know whose meeting it is.

| # | Story | Covers | Done when |

| 1 | **Book a 30-minute slot from today's page** (thin slice, end to end) | R1, R2, R3 | You start the app on your computer, book a free slot with your name and a title, reload, and see it booked with both shown. |
| 2 | **Bookings never overlap, even when made at the same moment** | R4, R5 | Tests pass for three cases: an overlapping booking is refused, an 11:00 end and an 11:00 start are both accepted, and of two simultaneous bookings exactly one wins while the other gets "This slot has just been booked." |
| 3 | **Choose a meeting length of 30, 60, 90 or 120 minutes** | R3, R4 | A 90-minute booking fills three slots on the page, and a length that runs into another booking is refused. |
| 4 | **Only today's remaining slots can be booked** | R1, R3 | Tests with a fixed clock show that past slots, bookings ending after 18:00, and bookings for other days are all refused. |

How I made the split:
- **Story 1 is the thin slice.** It sets up the app, the database with all five rooms, today's page and a booking. The length is fixed at 30 minutes because choosing a length is story 3 on its own, so story 1 doesn't carry a temporary shortcut. It's the only story marked as needing you, because you start the app and book through the browser.
- **Story 2 is second because it's the riskiest part.** The overlap check works on start and end times, not on individual 30-minute slots, so it already handles story 3's longer bookings.
- **All four stories change the same booking code**, so they run one after another and can't be built in parallel. The ticket script found no problems with the order or the dependencies.
- I recorded the decision to skip epics and the choice of story 1 as the thin slice in the initiative's Notes.

**The method's rules would add one thing:** a fifth story at the end, a cleanup pass over anything the first four put off. You asked for three or four, so I'd skip it and record that as a decision. You can add it later if the code gets messy.

**Say yes** and I'll commit this on `plan/meeting-room-booker`, with the cleanup story recorded as declined. After that, story 1 is ready to build with `bmad-build`.
